query: The (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 high-entropy alloy is a solid refrigeration working medium that exhibits a large caloric response under applied-field and pressure-field operation but has poor load-bearing integrity and tends to crack. What single intervention could increase its integrity while preserving caloric performance in these operating regimes? State one hypothesis specifying the intervention, its proposed mechanism, predicted integrity and caloric outcomes relative to the unchanged alloy, applicable field, pressure, temperature, and loading boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a controlled experiment with explicit results that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Introducing a small amount of interstitial nitrogen (≈0.5 at.%) during alloy synthesis will improve the load‐bearing integrity of the (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 high‐entropy alloy by strengthening the lattice (via increased stacking fault energy and enhanced grain boundary cohesion) without notably altering the order–disorder transition that underpins its caloric response.
generation.material_initial_state: The as‐synthesized (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 alloy shows a large caloric response under applied magnetic and pressure fields but suffers from poor load‐bearing integrity with a proneness to cracking during mechanical load.
generation.intervention: Add a low concentration (approximately 0.5 atomic percent) of nitrogen as an interstitial dopant during the alloy’s synthesis.
generation.conditions: The material is operated near room temperature under applied magnetic/pressure fields for caloric cooling applications and subjected to relevant mechanical loading conditions (tensile or bending tests) that mimic service environments.
generation.structural_mediator: Interstitial nitrogen atoms occupy sites in the alloy lattice, which increases the stacking fault energy and augments grain boundary cohesion while minimally affecting the order–disorder transition.
generation.mechanism: By raising the stacking fault energy, nitrogen reduces the tendency for excessive dislocation movement and premature crack initiation. This improved lattice integrity enhances toughness and load-bearing capacity while the underlying thermodynamic transformation (responsible for the caloric effect) remains largely intact.
generation.predicted_outcome: The nitrogen-doped alloy is expected to exhibit a statistically significant increase in fracture toughness and load-bearing strength (i.e., reduced cracking under stress) while maintaining a caloric response (entropy change and temperature shift under applied field/pressure) comparable to the undoped alloy.
generation.baseline: The undoped (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 alloy has excellent caloric properties but poor mechanical integrity and a tendency to crack under load.
generation.boundary: This intervention is predicted to be effective under room-temperature conditions with standard applied magnetic/pressure fields for caloric cooling. The doping level should remain near 0.5 at.% to avoid potential shifts in the caloric phase transition; higher or lower concentrations might compromise either mechanical or caloric performance.
generation.uncertainty: While nitrogen is expected to enhance mechanical robustness by modifying defect structures, the precise optimal concentration and its influence on the kinetics or magnitude of the caloric transition require further optimization. There is also some uncertainty regarding the interaction of nitrogen with the specific multi-element matrix of (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 alloy samples: one set with a controlled addition of ~0.5 at.% interstitial nitrogen and one set without doping. Characterize both sets using TEM and XRD to examine microstructural changes and measure the stacking fault energy. Perform mechanical tests (e.g., tensile, bending, fracture toughness tests) to assess load-bearing integrity and use caloric measurement techniques under identical applied magnetic and pressure fields (at room temperature) to quantify the entropy changes and temperature shifts.
measurements: Caloric effect magnitude (entropy change and adiabatic temperature change)
Microstructural features (grain boundary cohesion, dislocation behavior, stacking fault spacing)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the nitrogen-doped samples do not exhibit a statistically significant improvement (e.g., <10% increase) in mechanical integrity indicators (such as fracture toughness or tensile strength) compared to the undoped samples, or if the caloric response is reduced by a significant margin (e.g., >10% decrease in entropy change or temperature shift), then the hypothesis will be considered falsified.

cited_evidence.text: ABSTRACTWe investigated the effects of interstitial N and C on the stacking fault energy (SFE) of an equiatomic CoCrNi medium entropy alloy. Results of computer modeling were compared to tensile deformation and electron microscopy data. Both N and C in solid solution increase the SFE of the face-centered cubic (FCC) alloy matrix at room temperature, with the former having a more significant effect by 240% for 0.5 at % N. Total energy calculations based on density functional theory (DFT) as well as thermodynamic modeling of the Gibbs free energy with the CALPHAD (CALculation of PHAse Diagrams) method reveal a stabilizing effect of N and C interstitials on the FCC lattice with respect to the hexagonal close-packed (HCP) CoCrNi-X (X: N, C) lattice. Scanning transmission electron microscopy (STEM) measurements of the width of dissociated ½<110> dislocations suggest that the SFE of CoCrNi increases from 22 to 42–44 mJ·m−2 after doping the alloy with 0.5 at. % interstitial N.
